name: Zapatismo
summary: Zapatismo is the agrarian revolutionary outlook of Emiliano Zapata and the Liberation Army of the South in the Mexican Revolution. It held that land, water and woods taken by haciendas must be restored to the villages and that great estates must be broken up so every family can farm its own plot, communally or as small property. Around that core its intellectuals drafted a social state: recognition of unions and strikes, labour protections, public assistance as justice, municipal self-government, popular juries, plebiscites on laws and an armed people in place of a standing army.
scope: Emiliano Zapata's own Zapatismo, 1911-1919: the Plan of Ayala (1911), the Liberation Army of the South, the Morelos agrarian reform and 'commune' of 1914-1916, the Agrarian Law of 1915 and the other laws of the Zapatista-led Executive Council of the Convention (1915-1916), and Zapata's letters such as his 1918 letter on the Russian revolution, read with the historians cited (Ávila Espinosa, building on Womack, Rueda and others). Where the council's intellectuals went beyond what the movement practised (gradual socialisation, laicism, divorce), answers are lower confidence. It excludes the EZLN and 1990s neozapatismo, audited separately as neozapatismo.

keyFigures.name: Emiliano Zapata
keyFigures.role: Leader of the Liberation Army of the South and namesake of the ideology; signer of the Plan of Ayala.

keyFigures.name: Otilio Montaño
keyFigures.role: Co-author of the Plan of Ayala and the movement's main early intellectual; later in charge of public instruction.

keyFigures.name: Manuel Palafox
keyFigures.role: Zapatista secretary of agriculture who directed the Morelos land reform and drafted the 1915 Agrarian Law.

universal-healthcare.rationale: The Zapatista public-assistance law promised free medical care to those unable to work; universal healthcare for all is inferred from that welfare commitment.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: The Zapatista labour law set a minimum wage fixed yearly by local revolutionary reform boards, showing support for wage floors set to protect workers.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: The movement favoured a mixed economy with communal and state elements and blamed land monopoly for poverty; distrust of unregulated markets is inferred from that.

public-ownership.rationale: Zapatista laws of 1915 placed the Morelos sugar mills and other industry under public control and proposed a state bank; extending this to energy and rail is inferred.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: The programme wanted to tax foreign companies heavily and finance reform from enemies' property; a general higher tax on the rich is inferred from that.

unions-good.rationale: Zapatista delegates at the Convention won votes, against the Villistas, to give legal recognition to workers' organisations, strikes and boycotts.

property-fundamental.rationale: The Plan of Ayala ordered one-third of large estates expropriated and the whole property of opponents nationalised, treating landed property as overridable for justice.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Zapatista law made employers liable for accidents, set an eight-hour day and minimum wages, and allowed socialising harmful monopolies, which amounts to tighter control of business.

cut-welfare.rationale: The Zapatista public-assistance law made the state responsible for feeding, housing and caring for everyone unable to work, as a matter of justice rather than charity.

worker-ownership.rationale: The 1915 labour law aimed at the gradual socialisation of production through workers' cooperatives, though Ávila notes the wider movement never practised this; support is a leadership position.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Nothing in the sources speaks to surveillance; opposition is inferred from the movement's hostility to Díaz-era repression and its absolute press freedom law.

legalize-drugs.rationale: The movement's strict revolutionary morality suggests no sympathy for legal drug use; the answer is inferred and the sources do not discuss drugs.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: The Zapatista press law guaranteed absolute freedom of expression without censorship, so legal speech restrictions are inferred to be opposed.

strong-leader.rationale: The Plan of Ayala declares its authors 'partisans of principles and not of men' and repudiates Madero's personal rule, rejecting a leader above the law.

state-harmful.rationale: Despite anarchist influences on its slogans, Zapatismo set out to take power and build a new social state that guarantees land and labour rights, so it did not reject the state.

limit-guns.rationale: Zapatismo armed the villages and wanted the people in arms to replace the standing army, so strict gun limits run against its principles; the answer is inferred.

empower-police-military.rationale: The Zapatista council called the standing army 'an instrument of murder' used to oppress the people and legislated to abolish it.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: The sources do not discuss sex work; opposition is inferred from the movement's rigid revolutionary morality and its protective view of women.

decide-locally.rationale: The movement restored the authority of the pueblos and municipal autonomy and relied on municipalities to carry out reforms, though it kept agrarian reform under a central ministry.

rehabilitation.rationale: The Zapatista justice law held society responsible for crime and set up agricultural and industrial regeneration centres to rehabilitate offenders through work.

traditional-family.rationale: The village base was Catholic and traditional, while the leadership's marriage law recognised free unions and gave natural children equal rights; the two pull in opposite directions.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Never raised by a 1910s peasant movement; the answer is inferred from its traditional village base and is anachronistic.

abortion-legal.rationale: Abortion is absent from the sources; opposition is inferred from the Catholic peasant base and is anachronistic.

more-religion-public.rationale: The Plan of Ayala takes Juárez's laws against Church property as its model, suggesting Reform-era anticlericalism among its leaders even though followers were Catholic; the answer is inferred.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Montaño saw education as the means to raise the poor, above all the indigenous, and land restitution undid dispossession of Nahua villages; a general commitment to racial redress is inferred.

gender-social-construct.rationale: The council's laws treated women as the weaker party needing protection, which implies fixed views of gender; the question is anachronistic.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Zapatismo defended the customs and land of the old villages against haciendas and foreign capital; a broader cultural nationalism is inferred.

gradual-change.rationale: The Plan of Ayala calls Mexicans to take up arms, seize stolen lands at once and accept no compromise with the old regime.

reduce-immigration.rationale: The Zapatista colonisation law invited foreign as well as Mexican settlers to agricultural colonies, so immigration curbs are not supported; the answer is inferred.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: No international body existed to take a view on; the movement neither sought nor rejected one, so the answer is a neutral inference.

free-trade.rationale: The council wanted free trade in basic necessities while fostering national industry and opposing foreign investment, a mixed stance on trade.

nation-first.rationale: The movement was strongly nationalist and hostile to foreign investment, but Zapata also called the Mexican and Russian causes 'the cause of all humanity'; leaning nationalist is inferred.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Zapatismo resented foreign interference, including US backing for Carranza; opposition to foreign military intervention is inferred.

open-borders.rationale: Open borders were never discussed; the movement's nationalism suggests it would not support them, which is inferred.

limit-growth.rationale: The Zapatista programme sought to foster agriculture, credit and national industry, so limiting growth is not supported; the environmental question is anachronistic.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Climate change is anachronistic for a 1910s movement, and nothing in its principles points either way.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: The council wanted technical education and experimental farm stations, but its core problem was land monopoly, not technology; a neutral inference.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Nuclear power is anachronistic for the movement and nothing in its principles bears on it.

revolution-justified.rationale: The Plan of Ayala calls on Mexicans to support it 'with arms in hand' and pledges to continue the revolution until victory or death.

experts-over-public.rationale: Zapatista justice law sought to end lawyers' 'monopoly' of justice through popular juries, and laws were to be ratified by plebiscite, favouring the public over specialists.

central-planning.rationale: The movement's economy mixed communal, private small-holding and state elements rather than a planned economy; the answer is inferred from that mix.

socialized-markets.rationale: Leaders wanted cooperatives and municipally owned industry alongside small private property, which fits market exchange among socialised firms; the answer is inferred.

land-value-tax.rationale: Mendoza López blamed ground rent for poverty, a Georgist-like idea, but the movement chose expropriation and restitution rather than a land tax.

tax-inheritance.rationale: The labour law socialised industries whose owners died without heirs or will; heavy inheritance taxation in general is inferred.

basic-income.rationale: Zapatista law tied income to productive work and gave public assistance only to those unable to work, so an unconditional income is inferred to be rejected.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: The programme wanted to foster national industry yet also free trade in necessities; its stance on tariffs is unclear.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Zapatista plans had the agriculture ministry finance an agricultural bank, regional farm schools and experiment stations, and proposed a state bank to develop national industry.

widespread-small-property.rationale: The 1915 agrarian law gave every person a natural right to land for their family, capped holdings, and gave communal and small private property equal legal standing.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: The movement kept wage labour and set minimum wages; abolishing money was not on its agenda, so the answer is inferred.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Zapatista finance proposals included a state bank and monetary unification, the opposite of leaving money to the market.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Local reform boards set minimum wages and settled labour disputes, a state-recognised body, but not a joint employer-worker corporation; the fit is unclear.

one-party-rule.rationale: The Plan of Ayala calls for elections after victory and the Convention programme for direct suffrage; one-party rule is inferred to be rejected.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: A republican movement inspired by Juárez's Reform, Zapatismo had no place for hereditary rule; the answer is inferred.

democracy-best.rationale: The Plan of Ayala calls for elections to federal and state powers after victory, and the council held that real democracy means voters approve laws as well as choose rulers.

direct-votes.rationale: A council law required the fundamental laws of the republic to be ratified by plebiscite, defining real democracy as approving or rejecting laws by popular vote.

workers-councils.rationale: The Convention programme chose a parliamentary regime and direct suffrage, though local boards of the productive classes had real power; councils replacing parliament is inferred to be rejected.

right-to-secede.rationale: The Plan of Ayala invokes state sovereignty against Madero, but the movement sought a national government; secession was never discussed.

natural-rulers.rationale: The movement's egalitarian appeal to the oppressed and its rejection of personal rule suggest disagreement; the answer is inferred.

political-violence-never.rationale: Zapatismo was an armed movement whose founding plan orders villages to hold recovered land by force of arms.

war-builds-character.rationale: The council's antimilitarism and its call to abolish the army suggest no romance of war; the answer is inferred.

separate-church-state.rationale: The council's education law made primary schooling lay, and the Plan models itself on Juárez's Reform laws; Ávila notes laicism was the intellectuals' view more than the base's.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Zapatista laws rested on natural rights and revolutionary justice, not religion; the answer is inferred from that secular framing.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Zapatismo wanted popular juries and public gendarmeries run by the federation, states and municipalities, not private provision; the answer is inferred.

military-superiority.rationale: The movement wanted to abolish the standing army, which is inferred to rule out pursuing military superiority.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Zapatismo's appeal was to the oppressed classes and village communities, not to an ethnic nation; the answer is inferred.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Zapata's 1918 letter frames history as the awakening of oppressed peoples against exploiting landlords and warns of the bourgeoisie, a class reading though not a Marxist one.

equal-outcomes.rationale: The labour law spoke of building a social order based on justice and equality, but the movement kept small private property and did not seek to abolish classes; mild agreement is inferred.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: The Plan of Ayala restores land, woods and water to villages holding title to them, many of them Nahua communities that had held land in common.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Zapata likened foreign capital to Spanish colonial extraction but never asked Spain for reparations; the question does not map onto the movement.

civilizational-union.rationale: The movement had no project of uniting nations by religion; Zapata's internationalism was about oppressed classes, so the answer is inferred.

self-interest-moral.rationale: The leaders condemned landlords' greed and imposed a strict revolutionary morality on officials; the answer is inferred.

duties-before-rights.rationale: The movement spoke both of natural rights to land and of strict duties of revolutionary morality; neither clearly comes first.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Zapata described land, water and air as common property, but in terms of human use; intrinsic value of nature is not addressed.

limit-population.rationale: Zapatismo traced poverty to land monopoly, not numbers of people; opposition to population limits is inferred.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: The movement wanted modern farming, technical schools and national industry, so it did not reject industrial civilisation; the answer is inferred.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Support for technical education sits beside a defence of village life; there is no clear position on accelerating change.

human-enhancement.rationale: Human enhancement is anachronistic for the movement and nothing in its principles bears on it.

algorithmic-government.rationale: AI government is anachronistic for a 1910s movement and has no basis in its principles.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: Encryption is anachronistic for the movement; no position can be drawn from its principles.

restore-past-order.rationale: Recent historians reject the old view that Zapatismo only wanted to restore a golden age of village peace, yet restitution of lost lands was central.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Zapata's own headquarters governed pragmatically while the intellectuals wrote programmes; there is no stated view on this.

direct-action.rationale: The Plan of Ayala tells villages to take immediate possession of stolen land, rather than wait for courts or legislatures, though it also planned elections.

means-match-ends.rationale: The movement held arms and strict discipline justified by the goal of land reform; no explicit view on prefiguration exists.

return-to-foraging.rationale: An agrarian movement built on farming villages, Zapatismo would reject foraging; the answer is inferred.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Ávila describes a natural division of labour within the movement between farmers, soldiers and intellectuals; abolition was never sought.

distribute-by-need.rationale: The labour law promised workers the full product of their labour rather than distribution by need; the answer is inferred.

production-for-use.rationale: Zapata saw the land as property of all for subsistence, and leaders favoured cooperatives; production for need over profit is inferred.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Mendoza López counted industrialists and merchants among the productive classes and singled out only landlords as idle exploiters, so profit as such was not condemned.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: The movement wanted elections and a parliamentary regime and aimed only to eliminate the landlords, not to rule through a dictatorship of one class; the answer is inferred.

collective-farming.rationale: The Zapatista agrarian law gave communal and individual holdings equal legal status and left each community and person free to choose either.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Zapatismo did not hold a theory of imperialism; Zapata's letter does not mention it, so no position can be stated.

taxation-theft.rationale: The council restructured taxes and wanted heavy taxes on foreign firms, so it accepted taxation; it did call taxes on necessities and on labour obstacles to be removed.

harm-principle.rationale: The council's rigid morality and its scrutiny of officials' private lives suggest it would not limit the state to preventing harm; the answer is inferred.

individual-rights-only.rationale: The agrarian law recognised the rights of communities as well as individuals to restored land and to choose communal tenure.

conscription.rationale: The movement fought the federal levy and wanted an armed people instead of a permanent army; opposition to conscription is inferred.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Zapatismo sought to change Mexico through revolution and elections, not emigration; the answer is inferred.

state-as-business.rationale: The movement wanted a social state serving the needy classes, not a business model; the answer is inferred.

positive-liberty.rationale: Zapatismo held that freedom required land for subsistence: the agrarian law made the state guarantee each person's natural right to the land they need.

media-academia-power.rationale: The question is anachronistic and the sources say nothing about media or universities as a power.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Montaño saw education as the way to raise the indigenous poor, implying their condition was social not innate; the answer is inferred.

organic-representation.rationale: Zapatista practice relied on village and municipal councils, yet its programme also kept direct suffrage and a parliament; the fit is unclear.

total-state.rationale: The movement combined national coordination with decentralised municipal administration and absolute press freedom, not total state control; the answer is inferred.

national-rebirth.rationale: Zapatista rhetoric spoke of redeeming the oppressed rather than reviving a decadent nation; no clear position.

territorial-expansion.rationale: The movement was antimilitarist and focused on land within Mexico; expansion abroad is inferred to be rejected.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Despite strong personal loyalty to Zapata, the Plan of Ayala insists on principles not men; the answer is inferred.

bound-labor.rationale: Zapatismo rose against the hacienda system that tied peons to estates, and its agrarian law gave tenants and sharecroppers the land they worked.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: The sources contain no epistemological view; the justice law did say courts had served the powerful, which is not the same claim.

universal-morality.rationale: The Zapatista justice law describes laws as expressions of 'eternal and absolute precepts of justice'.

single-common-good.rationale: Zapatismo spoke of one justice but also defended specific class interests of the peasantry; no clear position.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: Entirely outside the movement's concerns; no position can be drawn.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: Diaspora return was never a concern of the movement and its principles give no answer.

revive-national-language.rationale: Language revival was never on the Zapatista agenda; no position can be inferred.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Leaders wanted socialised firms run by workers' cooperatives, which implies democratic control; the answer is inferred.

school-vouchers.rationale: The movement wanted free, compulsory public primary schooling run by federal, state and municipal governments, which is inferred to oppose vouchers.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Fiscal policy beyond tax reform was not discussed; no position can be stated.

economic-freedom.rationale: Zapatismo tied freedom to land ownership rather than to market freedom; the statement does not map onto its view.

rule-by-example.rationale: The council insisted that officials model honesty, live modestly and be watched by the people, giving weight to rulers' moral conduct; the answer is inferred.

national-self-determination.rationale: The movement defended Mexican sovereignty against foreign capital and US influence; a general principle is inferred.

force-without-un.rationale: The UN did not exist; the question is anachronistic and the movement's principles give no answer.

reason-over-faith.rationale: The leaders were liberal laicists while followers were devout Catholics; no stated view.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: The public-assistance law covered all human beings unable to work, without a citizenship test, but the question was never addressed directly.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Zapatista law reserved public assistance for those unable to work and reserved office for those who worked, suggesting the able should work; the answer is inferred.

class-collaboration.rationale: Leaders counted owners and workers alike as productive classes but backed strikes, boycotts and sabotage; the stance is mixed.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Nothing suggests the movement wanted to destroy cultural institutions; the answer is inferred.

dominated-front.rationale: Zapata hoped for solidarity among oppressed peoples, but in class not national terms; no stated view on a front of states.

workers-nation.rationale: Zapata appealed to the international proletariat and saw the Russian cause as Mexico's, which is inferred to favour international class ties.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Zapatista labour law barred women from night and underground work and treated them as needing protection, implying distinct roles; the answer is inferred.

ban-interest.rationale: The movement wanted agricultural banks and credit unions rather than a ban on interest; the issue is not addressed.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Nothing in the movement supports legal racial separation, and its base was mestizo and indigenous villagers; the answer is inferred.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Zapata wrote that landlords held land through 'the force of armies and the iniquity of the laws', and the council called the army a tool to oppress the people.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: The council discussed mining law and taxing foreign companies, but nothing on expanding oil or coal; no position.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Immigration was marginal to the movement; no position is documented.

elite-replacement.rationale: The movement blamed landlords for poverty, not immigration; the theory has no basis in its outlook and is anachronistic.

proportional-representation.rationale: Electoral systems were not discussed beyond direct suffrage; no position.

national-mission.rationale: Zapata's internationalism was solidarity with other revolutions, not a mission to impose Mexico's system; the answer is inferred.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: The marriage law saw women as the weaker party needing legal protection, but there is no theory of systematic male advantage; neutral.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: The Plan of Ayala denounces Madero as a traitor allied with the old científicos, and the council required officials to be watched by the people and barred from enriching themselves.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Eugenics never appears in the sources; the movement's view of crime and poverty as social suggests opposition, which is inferred.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: The movement opposed the federal army's repression and called it an instrument of murder; support for accountability is inferred.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The Zapatista programme gave the state duties of land reform, labour protection, public assistance and free schooling, far beyond a minimal state.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: The movement had no racial programme and drew on a mixed population; opposition is inferred.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The public-assistance law rejected charity as contrary to 'the equality of all men', and Zapata's letter speaks for all oppressed humanity.

socialism-one-country.rationale: Zapata praised the Russian revolution as humanity's cause but held no doctrine about socialism in one country.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Zapata compared foreign capital to Spanish colonial extraction but did not call Mexico a settler-colonial state; no clear position.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: The council's civil marriage law applied to all citizens in the Juárez liberal tradition; the answer is inferred.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Religious conversion is not discussed; the liberal Reform heritage suggests opposition, which is inferred.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: No basis in the movement's tradition; the answer is inferred.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Montaño's education law made public primary schooling free and lay, though Ávila says laicism was the intellectuals' view rather than the base's.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: Not a question the movement faced; no position can be drawn from the sources.

consent-of-governed.rationale: The Plan of Ayala condemns Madero for imposing governors on states against their will and calls for elected federal and state powers.

trade-surplus.rationale: Trade balances were not discussed by the movement; no position.

population-transfer.rationale: Expulsion of minorities was never proposed; the movement's targets were landlords' property, not peoples; the answer is inferred.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: The Plan of Ayala authorises villages to seize lands held by hacendados and defend them by arms, plainly endorsing force to achieve justice.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Zapatismo blamed greed and monopoly for misery and favoured cooperation; the answer is inferred.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Parties as such were not discussed; the Plan treats opponents as enemies but no rule on parties exists.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Zapatismo saw peasants subject to the arbitrary power of hacendados and bosses as unfree; the republican framing is inferred.

separated-powers.rationale: The Convention programme backed a parliamentary regime limiting the executive and wanted independent courts and popular juries; the answer is inferred.

vanguard-party.rationale: Zapatismo was a peasant army led by its own chiefs, not by a party; the answer is inferred.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Ávila concludes that Zapatismo wanted a state that attends first to the most numerous and unprotected classes.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Council housing did not exist; the question is anachronistic and the principles give no answer.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Zapatista delegates forced the Convention programme to recognise strikes, boycotts and even sabotage as legitimate workers' weapons.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Zapata blamed poverty on the monopoly of land by 'a few powerful individuals', and Mendoza López on landlords' rent.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: The movement's appeal crossed indigenous and mestizo lines; the answer is inferred.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: The justice law chose popular juries of ten by lot among literate citizens of each municipality; extending lottery to other offices is inferred.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: In wartime, justice was run by military chiefs, yet the programme guaranteed absolute press freedom; no stated position.

party-controls-media.rationale: The Zapatista press law guaranteed absolute freedom of expression without censorship, with disputes heard by popular juries.

notes: Historians distinguish the Zapatista headquarters' pragmatic, village-centred rule from the national programme written by its intellectuals (Palafox, Montaño, Mendoza López, Zubiría, Amezcua); Ávila Espinosa argues the programme was broadly representative but flags gradual socialisation, cooperatives, laicism and the marriage law as the intellectuals' own views, so those answers are low confidence. Many modern questions are anachronistic for a 1910s agrarian movement and are marked low. The EZLN (neozapatismo) is audited separately.
